name: Lexical Density (Content vs. Function Word Ratio)
description: Measures the proportion of content-bearing words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) against the total word count. AI text typically exhibits lower lexical density than expert human writing, as it relies heavily on functional 'glue' words to ensure smooth, highly probable grammatical transitions.
algorithm: POS (Part-of-Speech) Tagging & Content Word Ratio Calculation
mechanism: Lexical density is a fundamental computational linguistics metric dividing the number of 'content words' (which carry actual meaning) by the total number of words in a text. Expert human writers, particularly in academic or professional fields, tend to pack a high concentration of meaning into their sentences, resulting in a high lexical density (often above 50%). Large Language Models (LLMs), however, are optimized for probability and grammatical perfection rather than conciseness. To bridge concepts and maintain an authoritative, flowing tone, LLMs over-utilize 'function words'—articles (the, a), prepositions (in, on, concerning), conjunctions (and, however, furthermore), and pronouns. This creates a text that is syntactically beautiful but structurally diluted. The algorithm parses the text using a Part-of-Speech tagger, isolates all content words, and calculates the density percentage. If a seemingly sophisticated, long-form text registers an unusually low lexical density (indicating that it consists mostly of syntactical scaffolding rather than actual substance), it is flagged as characteristic of autoregressive padding.
useCase: Highly effective for auditing academic papers, professional reports, and essays. While it may falter on casual speech, it successfully exposes AI models that are attempting to mimic high-level academic writing but failing to match the expected information density.
strengths:
• Captures the hallmark 'flowery but empty' nature of AI writing, quantifying exactly why an AI text feels excessively lengthy.
• Computationally lightweight and fast, requiring only standard POS tagging.
• Highly resilient to minor prompt engineering, as LLMs cannot fundamentally rewrite their underlying probability distributions for functional grammar without breaking sentence coherence.
limitations:
• Naturally yields high false positive rates on transcripts of spoken human language, which inherently has a lower lexical density than written text.
• Heavily dependent on the language being analyzed; analytical languages (like English) have lower baseline densities than synthetic languages (like Russian or Finnish), requiring strict language-specific calibration.
• Can be bypassed if a human aggressively edits the text specifically to remove filler words, though this usually requires rewriting the entire document.
parameters:
Analysis: Part-of-Speech Target Filtering
Metric: (Total Content Words / Total Words) * 100
Output: 0-100 Lexical Dilution (Grammatical Padding) Score
accuracy: High — 78-85% on formal and academic text. It provides a reliable mathematical measurement of the structural 'fluff' inherent in LLM generation.

references.title: Ure, J. (1971). Lexical density and register differentiation. Applications of Linguistics.
Biber, D. (1988). Variation across speech and writing. Cambridge University Press.
